title: FREEDOM'S GROUND
subtitle: The South, 1865–1877
introBody: Emancipation has come, but freedom must be built — contested deed by deed, season by season. You are a newly freed person in the postwar South. The Freedmen's Bureau has opened its doors. Washington has made promises. And the men who once owned you are already writing new laws. Every choice you make will shape what freedom actually means in this county.
trailFeedOpener: Spring 1865: the war ends and the Bureau agent reads aloud General Order No. 3. You are free. What that means is still being decided.

events.title: Early Reconstruction — a Freedmen's Bureau meeting in your county seat
events.text: The Bureau agent has called freedpeople together to register labor contracts and hear grievances. You have walked miles to attend. Inside, a neighbor stands up and reads aloud, haltingly, the names of men who were beaten last week for leaving a planter's land under the terms a contract said they could. He asks everyone here to sign a letter to the Bureau's district superintendent — your names attached, visible, a formal complaint on record. Across the room a planter's overseer stands near the door taking note of who is present. You know what a signed name means in this county. You also know what silence has always meant.

choices.text: Walk to the front and sign the letter. Let your name stand with the others.
choices.result: This person, at the first real test, chose to be counted — to make their freedom a public fact that others could hold onto, whatever the cost of being seen.

choices.text: Stay seated. Do not sign. When the meeting ends, slip out before the overseer can mark your face to a name.
choices.result: This person, at the first real test, chose to protect what they could protect — calculating that survival of the private self was the only freedom they could actually hold onto, even if it meant leaving the public record bare.

events.title: Black Codes Posted at the Courthouse
events.text: The state legislature has passed its new laws. Vagrancy, labor contracts, apprenticeship — every clause tightens around freedpeople. The Bureau agent says he can file an objection if you bring him witnesses.

choices.text: Gather witnesses and file a formal Bureau objection.
choices.result: The superintendent forwards your complaint north. Three clauses are suspended by a federal officer. Your family wonders what comes next for pushing back so openly.

choices.text: Stay quiet. Work within the new terms for now.
choices.result: The codes take hold unopposed. You keep your head down and your family safer — for now. But neighbors notice who said nothing.

choices.text: Tell the Bureau agent; ask him to warn other freedpeople.
choices.result: Word spreads through the quarter. People know what they are facing. The Bureau agent thanks you for the intelligence.

trivia: Black Codes were passed by Southern state legislatures in 1865 and 1866 to restrict the rights of freedpeople.
The Freedmen's Bureau was created by Congress in 1865 to assist formerly enslaved people with contracts, education, and legal disputes.

events.title: Labor Contract Season
events.text: The planter's man arrives with a contract for the coming year. The terms give you a cabin and a share of the crop — but you cannot leave until harvest without forfeiting everything. The Bureau office is three hours' walk away.

choices.text: Walk to the Bureau office and have the agent review the contract.
choices.result: The agent crosses out two clauses that violate Bureau rules. You return with a better contract. The overseer watches you come back.

choices.text: Sign as written. It is better than vagrancy charges.
choices.result: You have shelter and work. The terms are hard, but your family is not arrested. What you gave up stays with you quietly.

choices.text: Refuse and seek land to rent independently.

outcomes.result: A freedman two counties over rents you a half-acre. Hard, but yours.
Every landowner in the county refuses you. Vagrancy charges follow within a week.

trivia: Freedmen's Bureau labor contracts were meant to protect freedpeople from exploitative terms, but enforcement depended on available agents.
Vagrancy laws under Black Codes could imprison freedpeople who were not under a labor contract, effectively restoring forced labor.

events.title: A School Needs a Building
events.text: A missionary teacher has arrived and wants to hold classes for children and adults. She needs a space. The AME church group says if you help them secure a building, the congregation will host school on Sundays.

choices.text: Donate your free days to help raise the building.
choices.result: Forty people show up the first Sunday. The teacher says it is the fastest school she has seen built. Your family sees less of you, but the community has a place.

choices.text: Offer your cabin for night classes — smaller risk.
choices.result: Six adults learn to read by December. It is modest, but real. Your family is part of it.

choices.text: Stay away. A school is a target, and you cannot afford it.
choices.result: The building goes up without you. You protect what you have. The neighbors remember who was not there.

trivia: African American churches were among the most important institutions freedpeople built during Reconstruction — anchors for education, mutual aid, and political organizing.
Northern missionary societies, including the American Missionary Association, sent teachers south after the war to establish freedpeople's schools.

image.artist: State Library and Archives of Florida

events.title: President Johnson's Veto
events.text: Word reaches the county: President Johnson has vetoed the bill extending the Freedmen's Bureau and the Civil Rights Act. The local Bureau agent looks shaken. He says his orders may not hold much longer.

sageAdvice.name: Bureau agent
sageAdvice.line: Congress may override him — but until they do, every order I give is on uncertain ground.

choices.text: Write to your congressman — document every Bureau case you know of.
choices.result: Congress overrides the veto. The Civil Rights Act of 1866 becomes law. Your letter was one of hundreds that moved a vote.

choices.text: Focus on the Bureau cases you can win right now, while the agent still has authority.
choices.result: You file three labor disputes and win two. The agent processes them before any change in orders arrives.

choices.text: Accept that Washington's protection has limits and build locally instead.
choices.result: The church mutual aid society doubles its membership. Federal protection shrinks, but neighbors watch out for each other.

trivia: President Andrew Johnson vetoed both the Freedmen's Bureau extension and the Civil Rights Act of 1866; Congress overrode both vetoes.
Johnson's lenient Reconstruction policy quickly restored former Confederate officials to power in Southern states.

events.title: Night Riders in the County
events.text: Three freedmen who registered voters last month have been beaten. The local sheriff refuses to investigate. The federal commander at the garrison says he needs written complaints from witnesses to act.

choices.text: Collect signed witness statements and deliver them to the federal garrison.
choices.result: Two riders are arrested under the military court. The terror slows — for now. Your name is known. Your wife says nothing, but she counts who has been watching the road.

choices.text: Warn the community privately without signing anything.
choices.result: People hear the warning. Three families move their meetings indoors. No formal record is made and no arrest follows.

choices.text: Do nothing. Any action makes you the next target.
choices.result: The riders return. Two more men are beaten. The garrison does not move without complaints. Your silence weighs on you.

trivia: The Ku Klux Klan used targeted violence against Black political organizers, teachers, and community leaders to suppress Reconstruction.
The Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871 gave the federal government power to prosecute Klan violence — but enforcement required political will and military presence.

image.artist: Originally published by the Toronto Star. Unknown author.

events.title: The Last Federal Troops Leave
events.text: The new president has ordered federal troops withdrawn from the state. The Freedmen's Bureau has already closed most of its offices. The men who call themselves Redeemers take the statehouse this week.

choices.text: Hold a community assembly. Document what was built and pledge to protect it.
choices.result: Fifty people gather in the church. The teacher reads the Fourteenth Amendment aloud. What was built here will not be surrendered without memory.

choices.text: Transfer property and records to the church — protect what can be protected.
choices.result: The deed is in the church's name. The school's records are hidden beneath the floorboards. Some things survive the storm.

choices.text: Move north while movement is still possible.
choices.result: You take your family out of reach. The people left behind face what is coming without you. You carry that with you.

trivia: The Compromise of 1877 ended Reconstruction by withdrawing the last federal troops from the South in exchange for Republican electoral votes.
After Reconstruction collapsed, former Confederate Democrats known as Redeemers took control of Southern state governments and systematically rolled back freedpeople's political rights.

events.title: Two years later — a night rider warning arrives at your door

text.default: Word comes before dawn: men on horses passed your neighbor's fence and left a burned post as a message. You have been named before — your signature is on record, your face is known at the courthouse. The community knows you as someone who stands. They come to you tonight not because you are brave but because you have already made yourself visible, and now that visibility is both the reason for the threat and the reason people believe something must be done together. You did not choose this moment. You chose the moment that made this one inevitable.

variants.text: Word comes before dawn: men on horses passed your neighbor's fence and left a burned post as a message. You have been named before — your signature is on record, your face is known at the courthouse. The community knows you as someone who stands. They come to you tonight not because you are brave but because you have already made yourself visible, and now that visibility is both the reason for the threat and the reason people believe something must be done together. You did not choose this moment. You chose the moment that made this one inevitable.

Word comes before dawn: men on horses passed your neighbor's fence and left a burned post as a message. Your name is not on the letter. You have been careful. But the burned post does not ask whose name is on what paper — it asks whose house sits on land that someone else wants. You have traded visibility for safety, and tonight the safety feels thinner than you believed it was. Your neighbor, the one whose name is on record, comes to ask if you will stand with them now, in the open, before it is too late. You have built something worth protecting. The question that has lived quietly inside you since the day of the meeting surfaces again.

choices.text: Go on.

sages.name: Oliver O. Howard
sages.title: Commissioner, Freedmen's Bureau
sages.bio: Oliver O. Howard commanded the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands from its founding in 1865. A Union general known as the 'Christian General,' he genuinely supported freedpeople's rights — but operated with too few agents, too little funding, and executive resistance from President Johnson.
sages.greeting: The Bureau agent says his superintendent is passing through and wants to speak with freedpeople directly. You walk to the office and find a tall man in a worn uniform behind the desk.
sages.advice: "The Bureau can do much — labor contracts, schooling, courts. But we need your testimony. Without it, I cannot act. Washington watches what we document."

question.question: What was the Freedmen's Bureau created to do?
choices: Redistribute all Southern plantation land to freedpeople
Help formerly enslaved people with contracts, education, and legal protection
Enforce loyalty oaths on Confederate soldiers
Manage railroad construction in the postwar South
question.explanation: The Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands (1865) assisted formerly enslaved people by negotiating labor contracts, establishing schools, and providing a legal forum when local courts refused freedpeople's testimony. It was underfunded and understaffed throughout its existence.
question.teksRef: TEKS 8.9 — Reconstruction: federal protection and the Freedmen's Bureau

sages.name: Hiram Revels
sages.title: U.S. Senator, Mississippi
sages.bio: Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first African American U.S. Senator in 1870, filling the seat once held by Jefferson Davis. An AME minister and educator, he represented what Congressional Reconstruction made briefly possible — Black political power at the highest levels of government.
sages.greeting: A man passing through your county stops to speak at the church. He has just come from Washington. Someone whispers that he sits in the United States Senate.
sages.advice: "What you build here — the school, the church, the vote — that is what I carry to Washington. They cannot dismiss it if it is real and documented and present."

question.question: What made Hiram Revels's election to the U.S. Senate in 1870 historically significant?
choices: He was the first senator from Mississippi after the war
He was the first African American to serve in the U.S. Senate
He wrote the Fourteenth Amendment
He commanded federal troops during Reconstruction
question.explanation: Revels became the first African American U.S. Senator in 1870, representing Mississippi. His election was made possible by the Fifteenth Amendment and Congressional Reconstruction's enforcement of Black voting rights — gains that were systematically reversed after federal protection collapsed.
question.teksRef: TEKS 8.9 — Reconstruction: African American political participation

sages.name: Thaddeus Stevens
sages.title: Radical Republican, U.S. House of Representatives
sages.bio: Thaddeus Stevens of Pennsylvania was the most powerful Radical Republican in Congress. He championed land redistribution — 'forty acres and a mule' — as the only economic foundation for freedpeople's real independence, and he led the impeachment of Andrew Johnson. His redistribution proposals were blocked by moderate Republicans.
sages.greeting: A pamphlet arrives from a traveling preacher — an old congressman's speech reprinted in full. The words inside are the fiercest you have read from any white man in Washington.
sages.advice: "Without land, freedom is a word on paper. The plantation system will reconstitute itself if freedpeople have no independent economic base. I have said this and been ignored. Do not ignore it yourselves."

question.question: Why did Thaddeus Stevens argue that land redistribution was essential to Reconstruction?
choices: He wanted to punish Confederate planters financially
Without land, freedpeople would remain economically dependent on the same planters who had enslaved them
Land grants would fund the Freedmen's Bureau
He believed freedpeople should be resettled in the North
question.explanation: Stevens argued that without land of their own, formerly enslaved people would have no economic independence and would be forced back into labor arrangements controlled by the same planter class. His redistribution proposals — forty acres from confiscated Confederate estates — were rejected by moderate Republicans who prioritized reconciliation with the South.
question.teksRef: TEKS 8.9 — Reconstruction: land reform, Radical Republicans, and the limits of federal policy

route.title: Freedom's Ground
route.description: The war is over. What freedom means in this county is still being contested, season by season.

eventTrivia.question: What did Black Codes do to freedpeople's legal rights?
choices: Guaranteed them the right to vote
Restricted their movement, labor, and legal standing
Gave them ownership of plantation land
eventTrivia.fact: Black Codes, passed by Southern legislatures in 1865–1866, restricted freedpeople's ability to move, own property, or refuse labor contracts — legally re-subordinating them despite emancipation.

eventTrivia.question: Which federal agency was set up to help freedpeople after the war?
choices: The Bureau of Indian Affairs
The Freedmen's Bureau
The U.S. Postal Service
eventTrivia.fact: The Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands — the Freedmen's Bureau — was created in 1865 to assist formerly enslaved people with labor contracts, education, and legal protection.

eventTrivia.question: What did vagrancy laws under Black Codes allow authorities to do?
choices: Arrest freedpeople who were not under a labor contract
Confiscate plantation land for freedpeople
Require planters to pay fair wages
eventTrivia.fact: Vagrancy laws classified freedpeople without labor contracts as vagrants, allowing their arrest and forced labor — effectively restoring plantation conditions under a different legal name.

eventTrivia.question: Why did President Johnson's vetoes weaken Reconstruction?
choices: They disbanded the Union Army
They blocked legislation protecting freedpeople's rights and extending Bureau authority
They transferred Southern land to Northern investors
eventTrivia.fact: Johnson vetoed the Freedmen's Bureau extension and the Civil Rights Act of 1866, undermining federal protection. Congress overrode both vetoes, but Johnson's actions emboldened Southern resistance.

eventTrivia.question: What was the Fourteenth Amendment's main guarantee for freedpeople?
choices: The right to vote
Equal citizenship and protection under the law
Land redistribution to formerly enslaved people
eventTrivia.fact: Ratified in 1868, the Fourteenth Amendment granted citizenship to all persons born or naturalized in the United States and guaranteed equal protection of the laws — directly overturning the Dred Scott decision.

eventTrivia.question: What role did African American churches play during Reconstruction?
choices: They served as headquarters for the Freedmen's Bureau
They were centers of education, mutual aid, and political organizing
They replaced local government courts
eventTrivia.fact: Black churches were the most durable institution freedpeople built — anchoring schools, mutual aid societies, and political meetings when federal institutions were absent or hostile.

eventTrivia.question: How did the Ku Klux Klan undermine Reconstruction?
choices: By lobbying Congress to repeal the Civil Rights Act
By using violence and terror to suppress Black political participation
By organizing labor strikes on plantations
eventTrivia.fact: The Klan used targeted violence against Black voters, officeholders, teachers, and organizers to destroy the political gains Reconstruction had created — especially where federal troops were absent.

eventTrivia.question: What was sharecropping, and why was it problematic for freedpeople?
choices: A form of land ownership that freedpeople purchased from the Bureau
A labor system that kept freedpeople in debt and dependent on planters
A federal program that distributed crop surpluses to freedpeople
eventTrivia.fact: Sharecropping replaced slavery with a cycle of debt: freedpeople farmed a planter's land in exchange for a share of the crop, but inflated supply costs and dishonest accounting kept them perpetually indebted and unable to leave.

eventTrivia.question: What did the Fifteenth Amendment guarantee?
choices: That freedpeople could own land in Southern states
That citizens could not be denied the vote based on race
That Confederate states had to ratify new constitutions
eventTrivia.fact: The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) prohibited denying the right to vote based on race, color, or previous condition of servitude — the constitutional foundation for Black political participation during Reconstruction.

eventTrivia.question: Why did Thaddeus Stevens believe land redistribution was necessary?
choices: To fund the Freedmen's Bureau schools
Because without land, freedpeople had no economic independence from planters
To compensate Union soldiers for their service
eventTrivia.fact: Stevens argued that unless freedpeople owned land, they would remain economically controlled by the same planter class — making political freedom hollow. His redistribution proposals were rejected by moderate Republicans.

eventTrivia.question: What happened to Reconstruction when federal troops were withdrawn in 1877?
choices: Southern states continued enforcing civil rights laws on their own
Redeemer Democrats took control of Southern governments and reversed freedpeople's gains
The Freedmen's Bureau expanded its operations
eventTrivia.fact: The Compromise of 1877 ended federal military presence in the South. Redeemer Democrats quickly dismantled Black political representation, disenfranchised Black voters, and imposed the legal and economic subordination that became the Jim Crow era.

eventTrivia.question: What was the Compromise of 1877?
choices: A deal in which Republicans withdrew federal troops from the South in exchange for electoral votes
A treaty between former Confederates and the Freedmen's Bureau
A law that ended sharecropping in three Southern states
eventTrivia.fact: The Compromise of 1877 resolved the disputed 1876 presidential election: Republicans kept the White House, but federal troops were withdrawn from the South — effectively ending Reconstruction and leaving freedpeople without federal protection.

eventTrivia.question: What made Hiram Revels's service in the U.S. Senate historically important?
choices: He was the first senator to advocate for land redistribution
He was the first African American to serve in the U.S. Senate
He wrote the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871
eventTrivia.fact: Revels's 1870 election to the Senate — filling the seat once held by Jefferson Davis — demonstrated what federal protection of Black voting rights made possible. His presence was erased after Reconstruction collapsed.

eventTrivia.question: Why did Southern resistance to Reconstruction grow stronger over time?
choices: Because Congress reduced civil rights protections each year
Because federal enforcement weakened as Northern political will eroded, making resistance less costly
Because freedpeople stopped using the Freedmen's Bureau
eventTrivia.fact: Southern resistance intensified as Northern voters grew tired of Reconstruction's costs and as federal troop levels fell. Each reduction in enforcement signaled to planters and paramilitary groups that resistance would go unpunished.

eventTrivia.question: What were apprenticeship laws under the Black Codes designed to do?
choices: Train freedpeople for skilled trades
Allow courts to bind freedpeople's children to planters as unpaid laborers
Provide freedpeople's children with access to public schools
eventTrivia.fact: Apprenticeship laws allowed local courts to remove children from freedpeople's families and assign them to former slaveholders as bound laborers — separating families and restoring plantation labor through the legal system.

eventTrivia.question: What did the Civil Rights Act of 1866 do that was historically unprecedented?
choices: It banned the Ku Klux Klan
It declared all persons born in the United States to be citizens with equal legal rights
It gave freedpeople the right to vote in federal elections
eventTrivia.fact: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 was the first federal law to define citizenship and guarantee equal legal rights regardless of race — directly challenging Black Codes and setting the foundation for the Fourteenth Amendment.

historicalContext: Reconstruction (1865–1877) was a genuine but incomplete attempt to build a multiracial democracy in the postwar South. Federal will and freedpeople's legal standing were interdependent — neither could hold without the other. Community resilience, built through churches, schools, and mutual aid, proved to be the only durable foundation when federal protection collapsed. Southern resistance was not inevitable: it was sustained by inaction in Washington and unpunished violence on the ground. Every uncontested Black Code and every unanswered act of terror was a step toward the Redeemer period — legal freedom without practical protection — and toward the century of Jim Crow that followed.

family.default: Your family remembers a person caught between duty and love, doing what they could.

variants.text: They remember you as the one who kept them safe when safety was rare. The children know your face as shelter. Whatever else happened, you were there.
They remember you as someone pulled in two directions who did not always land on their side — but tried. The love was real, even when the choices were hard.

They remember your absence more than your presence. The cause, the neighbors, the fight — it took you from them in ways that could not always be repaid. They do not blame you. They just remember what was missing.

community.default: The community holds your memory as part of the larger story of what was attempted here.

variants.text: They remember you as someone who showed up — who put their name on the paper, stood in the meeting, helped raise the building. When the records of this time are read, yours is a name that held.
They remember you as someone who helped when they could and stepped back when they couldn't — a neighbor, not a leader. The community survived; you were part of that, in quiet ways.
They remember you as someone who was there but not present — who protected your own while others bore the cost of standing up. They do not speak ill of you. They just do not speak of you.
